interactions.label: In the pathogenesis of atherosclerosis, LDL particles that undergo oxidative mod

params.question: In the pathogenesis of atherosclerosis, LDL particles that undergo oxidative modification in the subendothelial space contribute to plaque formation primarily by:

answers.text: Stimulating hepatic LDL-receptor upregulation to clear excess circulating cholesterol

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Hepatic LDL-receptor upregulation is actually a beneficial mechanism that clears LDL from the blood. Ox-LDL forms within the vessel wall and is NOT cleared by hepatic receptors — instead it is taken up by macrophage scavenger receptors, which cannot be down-regulated by intracellular cholesterol levels.

answers.text: Directly constricting coronary arteries through endothelin release from damaged endothelium

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Although endothelial dysfunction occurs in atherosclerosis, endothelin-mediated vasoconstriction is not the primary mechanism by which ox-LDL drives early plaque formation. The key early event is foam-cell formation via unregulated macrophage uptake of ox-LDL.

answers.text: Being engulfed by macrophages via scavenger receptors to form foam cells — the basis of the fatty streak

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Correct. Macrophages engulf ox-LDL via scavenger receptors (e.g. SR-A, CD36) that, unlike hepatic LDL receptors, cannot be down-regulated by intracellular cholesterol. The resulting lipid-laden macrophages (foam cells) accumulate to form the fatty streak — the earliest visible atheromatous lesion.

answers.text: Activating the extrinsic coagulation pathway to generate thrombin on the plaque surface

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Thrombin generation and thrombosis occur when an advanced plaque ruptures (the basis of acute coronary syndromes), but this is a late complication. The earliest step in atherogenesis is ox-LDL uptake by macrophages to form foam cells, not coagulation activation.

overallFeedback.feedback: Review the oxidative-modification pathway: LDL enters the subendothelium → undergoes oxidation → ox-LDL is engulfed by macrophage scavenger receptors (which cannot be down-regulated) → foam cells → fatty streak — the earliest atheromatous lesion.

Excellent. The oxidative-modification hypothesis is central to understanding why LDL lowering reduces cardiovascular events — fewer LDL particles entering the subendothelium means less ox-LDL and fewer foam cells.

interactions.label: A patient with established atherosclerotic cardiovascular disease is already on

params.question: A patient with established atherosclerotic cardiovascular disease is already on the maximally tolerated statin dose but has not reached the LDL-C target. According to the step-up algorithm, what should be added next?

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Gemfibrozil is a fibrate primarily indicated for hypertriglyceridaemia, not for additional LDL lowering. It significantly increases the risk of statin-induced myopathy by inhibiting statin glucuronidation and should be avoided in combination with statins — use fenofibrate if a fibrate is needed.

Correct. Ezetimibe inhibits intestinal cholesterol absorption via NPC1L1, providing an additional 15–20% LDL-C reduction when added to a statin. It is the recommended first add-on agent — oral, well-tolerated, and more cost-effective than PCSK9 inhibitors.

PCSK9 inhibitors achieve potent LDL reduction (50–60%), but per the step-up algorithm they are the third step — reserved for patients who remain above target after maximally tolerated statin PLUS ezetimibe, particularly in familial hypercholesterolaemia or very-high-risk patients.

Cholestyramine (a bile-acid sequestrant) provides only modest LDL reduction (15–30%) and may paradoxically worsen hypertriglyceridaemia. It is not part of the recommended step-up algorithm for patients already on maximally tolerated statins.

overallFeedback.feedback: Remember the step-up algorithm: first add ezetimibe (oral, inexpensive, well-tolerated) to maximally tolerated statin; then, if still not at LDL target, add a PCSK9 inhibitor (injectable, expensive, reserved for high-risk or familial hypercholesterolaemia patients).
Well done. The step-up sequence — statin → add ezetimibe → add PCSK9 inhibitor — is a key prescribing framework for secondary prevention in dyslipidaemia management.

interactions.label: Ranolazine, used as add-on therapy in refractory chronic stable angina, produces

params.question: Ranolazine, used as add-on therapy in refractory chronic stable angina, produces its anti-ischaemic effect by which mechanism?

answers.text: Releasing nitric oxide to cause venodilation and reduce cardiac preload

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: This describes the mechanism of organic nitrates (GTN, ISDN, ISMN). Nitrates are NO donors that cause venodilation (reducing preload) and, at higher doses, arteriolar dilation (reducing afterload), thereby decreasing myocardial oxygen demand.

answers.text: Blocking L-type calcium channels in coronary vascular smooth muscle

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: This describes dihydropyridine calcium channel blockers (e.g. amlodipine, nifedipine), which dilate coronary and peripheral arteries by blocking voltage-gated L-type calcium channels in vascular smooth muscle.

answers.text: Selectively reducing heart rate by blocking If channels in the sinoatrial node

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: This describes ivabradine, which selectively inhibits the If (funny) current in the SA node to reduce heart rate without affecting myocardial contractility or blood pressure — used when beta-blockers are contraindicated or insufficient.

answers.text: Inhibiting the late sodium current, thereby reducing intracellular sodium and calcium overload

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Correct. Ranolazine selectively inhibits the late sodium current (INa-late). By reducing intracellular Na⁺ accumulation, it decreases Ca²⁺ overload via the Na⁺–Ca²⁺ exchanger, improving diastolic relaxation and reducing ischaemia — without significantly affecting heart rate or blood pressure.

overallFeedback.feedback: Ranolazine inhibits the late sodium current (INa-late) → less intracellular Na⁺ → less Ca²⁺ via the Na⁺–Ca²⁺ exchanger → improved diastolic relaxation and reduced ischaemia. Distinguish from: nitrates (NO donors), CCBs (L-type Ca²⁺ channel blockers), and ivabradine (If channel blockers).
Excellent. Ranolazine's unique late-Na⁺-channel mechanism makes it valuable as add-on therapy because it reduces ischaemia without haemodynamic effects — no hypotension or reflex tachycardia.

interactions.label: Direct oral anticoagulants (DOACs) require routine coagulation monitoring simila

params.question: Direct oral anticoagulants (DOACs) require routine coagulation monitoring similar to warfarin.

l10n.wrongAnswerMessage: This statement is false. DOACs do NOT require routine coagulation monitoring. Warfarin has a narrow therapeutic index affected by many drug and dietary interactions, necessitating regular INR checks (target 2–3). DOACs, by contrast, have predictable dose–response pharmacokinetics and are given at fixed doses without laboratory surveillance — a key practical advantage over warfarin.
l10n.correctAnswerMessage: Correct — this statement is false. Unlike warfarin, which requires regular INR monitoring (target 2–3) due to its narrow therapeutic index and numerous drug–food interactions, DOACs (dabigatran, rivaroxaban, apixaban, edoxaban) have predictable pharmacokinetics and are prescribed at fixed doses without routine coagulation monitoring. This monitoring-free advantage is a major reason DOACs are now preferred over warfarin in many indications.

interactions.label: A 62-year-old woman with atrial fibrillation secondary to rheumatic mitral steno

params.question: A 62-year-old woman with atrial fibrillation secondary to rheumatic mitral stenosis requires long-term anticoagulation for stroke prevention. Which agent is most appropriate?

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Although apixaban has the best evidence among DOACs for non-valvular AF (ARISTOTLE trial — superior to warfarin for both efficacy and bleeding safety), DOACs are NOT recommended in AF associated with rheumatic mitral stenosis. They have not been shown to be effective in this population.

Dabigatran (a direct thrombin inhibitor) is not suitable here. The RE-ALIGN trial specifically showed that dabigatran was inferior to warfarin in patients with mechanical heart valves, and DOACs as a class are not recommended in rheumatic valvular AF.

Rivaroxaban (a direct Factor Xa inhibitor) is first-line for non-valvular AF but is not recommended in AF with rheumatic mitral stenosis. Warfarin remains the standard of care for this specific indication.

Correct. Warfarin remains the anticoagulant of choice in AF associated with rheumatic mitral stenosis or mechanical heart valves. DOACs have not been adequately studied in rheumatic valvular disease and are considered inadequate — the RE-ALIGN trial confirmed DOAC inferiority in mechanical valves.

overallFeedback.feedback: Key rule: DOACs are first-line for non-valvular AF (apixaban preferred — ARISTOTLE), but warfarin remains the standard for AF with rheumatic mitral stenosis or mechanical heart valves. The RE-ALIGN trial confirmed DOAC inadequacy in valvular disease.

Well done. Remembering that DOACs are first-line ONLY in non-valvular AF, while warfarin remains essential for rheumatic mitral stenosis and mechanical heart valves, is a critical prescribing distinction.
